lessons.title: Build a testing strategy
lessons.concept: Quality is a chain of evidence: an explicit expectation, a reproducible experiment, and a result compared with that expectation. In “Build a testing strategy”, the concrete input is cart-line total calculation for normal, zero, and invalid quantities. test pyramid means: A distribution with many fast tests, some integration tests, and few full journeys. The model is complete only when you test the pure rule with boundary values, then reserve browser journeys for contracts between components and can observe that the node --test report shows two passing tests and a future invalid case fails for the intended reason.

explanation.title: Simple analogy
explanation.text: A test is like a marker sealed before renovation: it does not build the house, but immediately reveals whether the work moved an important wall. Here the part you will actually inspect is a small Node suite that protects cart-line calculation; stop using the analogy if it obscures the technical boundary shown by the code.

explanation.title: Understand it deeply
explanation.text: Start by bounding this lesson’s case: cart-line total calculation for normal, zero, and invalid quantities. Distinguish unit, integration, and journey tests so each proof lives at the least expensive level. The term test pyramid is not a decorative label: A distribution with many fast tests, some integration tests, and few full journeys. It determines what enters, which authority may act, and which observation counts as evidence rather than an impression.

explanation.title: Understand it deeply
explanation.text: In exercises/19-quality/price.test.mjs, the example deliberately reduces the system to a small Node suite that protects cart-line calculation. Read each line as one responsibility, then run node --test exercises/19-quality/price.test.mjs. The main failure to trigger is: a rounding change breaks the total but no test close to the rule reports it. It shows why the professional correction is to test the pure rule with boundary values, then reserve browser journeys for contracts between components, not to conceal the error.

explanation.title: Understand it deeply
explanation.text: In a real system, the happy path is only one case among retries, invalid input, and partial outages. The expected proof is that the node --test report shows two passing tests and a future invalid case fails for the intended reason. Apply the same evidence to cart totals, order transitions, and administrator authorization, using a correlation trace without secrets or personal data so both success and failure remain explainable.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: A test is like a marker sealed before renovation: it does not build the house, but immediately reveals whether the work moved an important wall. Here the part you will actually inspect is a cart calculation split into named functions with a regression assertion; stop using the analogy if it obscures the technical boundary shown by the code.

Start by bounding this lesson’s case: an overly compact cart calculation whose line and aggregate totals must be separated without changing 398. Lock down current behavior, extract one responsibility at a time, and verify the same contract after every small change. The term refactoring is not a decorative label: Improving internal structure without changing observable behavior. It determines what enters, which authority may act, and which observation counts as evidence rather than an impression.

In exercises/19-quality/refactor-total.ts, the example deliberately reduces the system to a cart calculation split into named functions with a regression assertion. Read each line as one responsibility, then run npx tsc --noEmit. The main failure to trigger is: the refactor adds a discount rule at the same time, making the changed result impossible to attribute. It shows why the professional correction is to capture behavior first, rename or extract one responsibility, run the proof, and only then continue, not to conceal the error.

In a real system, the happy path is only one case among retries, invalid input, and partial outages. The expected proof is that the regression assertion and existing tests produce the same values before and after every extraction. Apply the same evidence to cart totals, order transitions, and administrator authorization, using a correlation trace without secrets or personal data so both success and failure remain explainable.
